subtitulo: Only, even, just — where they sit at the counter
descripcion: At C1 the focus is on adverbs that shift the meaning of the whole sentence depending on their position: only, even, just. Placed differently, the same words emphasise a different part of the sentence entirely — a precision tool, not just a rule to follow.

filas: she didn't fix it, just noticed

ejemplos.texto: Only the manager was informed about the change.
She had only just started when the call came in.
Even the experts couldn't explain it.

notas: Moving only one word changes which part of the sentence is being restricted or emphasised.
Even goes directly before the element it emphasises, whether that's the subject, the verb or the object.
In careful writing, these adverbs are placed precisely; in speech, intonation often does some of the work instead.

es.en: Spanish achieves this kind of emphasis by reordering the sentence or using solo more flexibly, without position changing the meaning so systematically. Spanish speakers tend to put only at the start of the sentence by default and lose the ability to focus a specific word in the middle.
es.es: El español consigue este tipo de énfasis reordenando la oración o usando «solo» con más libertad, sin que la posición cambie el significado tan sistemáticamente. Los hispanohablantes tienden a poner «only» al principio por defecto y pierden la capacidad de enfocar una palabra concreta en medio de la oración.

de.en: German focus particles stand directly before the focused element (Ich habe ihn nur gestern gesehen), so German speakers place only with great precision. This is correct in careful writing, but in spoken English only usually sits before the verb (I only saw him yesterday), and German speakers can sound over-precise.
de.de: Deutsche Fokuspartikeln stehen direkt vor dem fokussierten Element («Ich habe ihn nur gestern gesehen»), daher setzen Deutschsprachige «only» oft sehr präzise. Das ist in sorgfältiger Schriftsprache korrekt, kann im gesprochenen Englisch aber überpräzise wirken, wo «only» meist vor dem Verb steht («I only saw him yesterday»).

it.en: Italian solo usually stands before the verb or participle (ho solo visto), which matches spoken English well (I only saw). The typical Italian trap is anche, which means both also and even: Italian speakers write also where English needs even.
it.it: «Solo» in italiano sta di solito prima del verbo o del participio («ho solo visto»), che corrisponde bene all'inglese parlato («I only saw»). Il tipico tranello è «anche», che può significare sia «also» sia «even»: gli italofoni usano «also» dove l'inglese richiede «even».

fr.en: French ne… que places the restriction directly before the focused element (je ne l'ai vu qu'hier), which corresponds to careful written English (I saw him only yesterday). The typical trap is même, which means even, same and -self, and is easily mistranslated.
fr.fr: «Ne… que» place la restriction directement devant l'élément focalisé («je ne l'ai vu qu'hier»), ce qui correspond à l'anglais écrit soigné («I saw him only yesterday»). Le piège typique est «même», qui peut signifier «even», «same» ou «-self» et se traduit facilement de travers.

pt.en: Portuguese só usually stands before the verb (só o vi ontem), which matches spoken English. The typical trap is até, which means both even and until: Portuguese speakers may write until he came when they mean even he came.
pt.pt: «Só» costuma vir antes do verbo («só o vi ontem»), o que combina bem com o inglês falado. A armadilha típica é «até», que pode significar «even» ou «until»: falantes de português podem escrever «until he came» quando querem dizer «even he came».

errores: Always placing only at the start of the sentence, regardless of what should actually be emphasised.
Misplacing even so it modifies the wrong part of the sentence.
Relying on intonation alone in writing, where position is what actually carries the meaning.

es: Fronting *especially* as with *sobre todo*: *Especially I like jazz* instead of *I especially like jazz*.
de: Placing a time adverb between the auxiliary and the participle: *I have yesterday finished the report* instead of *I finished the report yesterday*.
it: Fronting *especially* as with *soprattutto*: *Especially I like jazz* instead of *I especially like jazz*.
fr: Fronting *especially* as with *surtout*: *Especially I like jazz* instead of *I especially like jazz*.
pt: Fronting *especially* as with *sobretudo*: *Especially I like jazz* instead of *I especially like jazz*.

traducciones.pt: o serviço de apoio ao cliente

redemittel.expresion: Move it and the emphasis moves.

traducciones.es: Si lo movés, se mueve el énfasis.
traducciones.de: Verschiebt man es, verschiebt sich die Betonung.
traducciones.it: Se lo sposti, si sposta l'enfasi.
traducciones.pt: Se o mudares de sítio, muda a ênfase.

mision.consigna: Write instructions for a newcomer on how to deal with a local registration office.
requisitos: *only* in three positions with three meanings
use *to fill in the form*, *red tape* and *customer service*

microtareas.texto: Write *I only need a copy of the form* and move *only* four times. Note what changes.
Five sentences about *a helpline* using *even* in different positions.
Record 90 seconds explaining who you would ask *to escalate a complaint* at an office you've been to.

autochequeo: Does the position of only match what I actually want to restrict?
Is even placed directly before the element it emphasises?
Would moving the adverb change the intended meaning?
Have I used position rather than relying only on intonation in writing?
Are at least three different positions of these adverbs used deliberately?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the position of only, even and just. Check whether each position matches the intended emphasis and flag any sentence where the position seems accidental. Do not rewrite the text.
